title: What We Heard From the Creative Commons Community
content:
It’s a question we ask ourselves regularly at CC—and one we recently brought directly to our community through our annual Community Survey. This year, 62 community members from 23 countries shared their experiences, priorities, ideas, and hopes for the future of the Commons.

What we heard most clearly is that you want  to participate. You want to learn from one another, contribute your skills, build relationships across regions and areas of practice, and help shape the future of the open movement. 

The survey gave us a clear picture of what meaningful participation means to you, what the barriers are, and what CC can do to help. Here’s what we heard and how it’s shaping our plans for the year ahead. 

A community that wants to participate

Overall satisfaction with the CC community increased this year, reaching 3.8 out of 5—up 19% from 2025. Sixty-four percent of respondents rated their engagement with the community a 4 or 5, and 60% said you would recommend the CC community to others.

Perhaps most encouragingly, half of you said you were interested in participating in self-led activities like ad-hoc working groups.

title: Openness & Digital Sovereignty: Who Sustains the Commons?
content:
We are in a critical moment for the open web, and must raise the issues of openness and the commons to the level of public dialogue as we try to steer AI development to serve the public interest. We are also in a moment when open is being hailed as a panacea for digital sovereignty. This warrants interrogation.

On September 21st, Creative Commons convened leading experts, practitioners, and builders for a day of conversation about the collaborative underpinnings of openness, investigating all the layers of the stack for a better, shared understanding of what openness can—and cannot—do to help communities and nations drive towards digital sovereignty.

This event was made possible through the generous support of the Siegel Family Endowment. We are grateful to our co-hosts at the NYU Engelberg Center for making the space for a conversation like this.

Clear throughlines from the convening were:

  • Openness creates choices
  • Sovereignty depends on our ability to exercise and sustain those choices
  • Sustaining the people, institutions, and shared resources that make openness possible must be part of any sensible sovereignty strategy

title: From Reflection to Action: 8 Hot Takes from CC’s Open Heritage Roundtable
content:
At our Open Heritage Dialogue held at UNESCO House last April, we had convened to find answers to an important question: How can equitable access to heritage help solve global challenges? What we heard was that it can in a diversity of ways: from supporting access to education to strengthening social inclusion and spurring artistic creativity, all the way to helping find concrete solutions to fight climate change. 

Five months later, on 29 September, we returned to Paris ready to move the conversation forward. Together with the Representation of Québec within the Permanent Delegation of Canada to UNESCO, we brought together around 30 participants to our Open Heritage Roundtable to discuss possible ways forward at UNESCO, with whom CC is an NGO in official partnership (consultative status). Participants hailed from UNESCO permanent delegations, UNESCO national commissions, national government and ministries of culture, national libraries and archives, international NGOs from the open heritage community, including the Open Heritage Coalition, among others, and their interventions were made in French and English.

title: A Principled Approach as the Sands Shift
content:
Creative Commons has been exploring questions around artificial intelligence for a long time: how this profound technological shift might affect people’s motivations to share, whether the intentions behind sharing work before AI became mainstream still hold when we consider how those works are being used now, and how we sustain a thriving commons when the fundamental bargain of the open web has shifted.

Throughout these changes, we have been guided by a commitment to balance creator agency in how people participate in the commons, while preserving the public’s right to reuse. CC licenses operate through copyright, and in many jurisdictions, copyright exceptions and limitations may permit certain AI development and training uses. That can leave people who want to share openly with limited ways to impose conditions, leading some to resort to restricting access instead. This risks pushing us towards an all-or-nothing binary between a free-for-all or enclosure. We fear the end result will be a retracted knowledge commons.

So we’ve been revisiting some fundamental questions:

  • When are norms enough, and when are enforceable conditions needed?

title: Guidance for Indigenous Collections and Data
content:
Creative Commons (CC) is happy to announce the launch of a new publication entitled Guidance for Indigenous Collections and Indigenous Data: Recommendations from Creative Commons and Local Contexts. This publication is the result of a collaboration with Local Contexts, as both organizations share commitments to equitable knowledge sharing, proper attribution, and respect for diverse cultural and community protocols. It aims to support cultural heritage institutions (CHIs) in navigating the complex legal, ethical, and cultural issues regarding open access to Indigenous heritage and associated data. 

In this blog post, we offer some background to the publication, share some hot takes from the launch webinar, and invite you to learn more about this topic.

title: Guidance on Using CC Licenses in an AI Ecosystem
content:
Since 2002, Creative Commons (CC) licenses have served as legally enforceable tools for digital sharing. Beyond their functionality, they also signal a commitment to open sharing in the public interest. 

CC’s general guidance has been to acknowledge and support all valid uses for each of our current six licenses and two public domain tools.  

When making decisions about which CC tool to use, we’ve long encouraged licensors to share their work under the most flexible CC license or tool applicable, while recognizing that some contexts call for added restrictions. This practice fosters robust knowledge and cultural exchange, which in turn strengthens our collective commons. Access to educational, scientific, and cultural content remains essential to society. 

However, that guidance was developed for a world of reuse by people, a premise that doesn’t fit as neatly in a world of widespread machine use of content through AI. 

So we went back to our own guidance and asked, “Does this still hold up?”

The short answer is: yes. 

You might be surprised that this guidance hasn’t substantially changed from what we’ve given in previous resources, even as AI reshapes how content and data is being used.

title: Open Heritage in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
content: Cultural heritage institutions (CHIs) such as museums, libraries, and archives, carry the important public-interest mission of providing access to the heritage in their collections. Their mission is grounded in broad public access and extensive human engagement, the existence of a vibrant cultural commons, and heritage enjoyed as a shared resource. CHIs understand that, as a representation of who we are, heritage helps define our shared humanity and that providing access to heritage generates numerous benefits for society. As such, CHIs, as stewards of trustworthy information imbued within knowledge and culture, have a crucial role to play in growing and protecting the commons and enabling uses that benefit humanity.

title: Creative Commons to Convene “A Conversation on Collaboration” Alongside UNGA 81
content:
As the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) convenes its 81st session in New York in September, Creative Commons is bringing together leading civil society and digital rights organizations for “A Conversation on Collaboration,” a day-long symposium examining how to balance digital sovereignty with open collaboration.

Alongside co-organizers Public Knowledge, Ushahidi, Project Liberty Institute, the Engelberg Center, the Global Solutions Initiative, and the AI Disclosures Project, CC will be adding to conversations that governments, the European Union, and the United Nations have been having this year. 

Open source and digital sovereignty are closely related. While open source does not suffice for digital sovereignty, it is a critical building block. While definitions of digital sovereignty vary, it is generally accepted that digital sovereignty at the national level entails the ability to independently control everything from infrastructure, to hardware, to software, to data.

The day’s conversations will work through questions including:

  • Where are open practices complementary, and where is there friction?

title: Announcing Four Regional Events for CC’s 25th Anniversary
content:
We are excited to announce that we will be supporting four regional events for CC’s 25th Anniversary—representing regions around the world with groups who are working to advance open knowledge. We’re delighted to be working with a variety of trusted partners and look forward to sharing more about their plans and reporting back on how these events went. 

We want to thank everyone who submitted a proposal for an event. There were so many great ideas, and we hope to have more opportunities to support regional work like this in the future. 

In Córdoba, LibreBase will celebrate 25 years of Creative Commons alongside Argentina’s longstanding cultura libre, free software, and open knowledge communities. The one-day gathering will bring together creators, educators, researchers, publishers, technologists, and activists for conversations and hands-on workshops exploring the impact of open licensing across culture, education, and knowledge. Participants can explore a showcase and digital swap of CC-licensed works, learn about remixing and Wikimedia Commons, and join a closing conversation on the future of the digital commons including emerging questions around generative AI.

title: 25 Years of Partnership: CC at Wikimania 2026
content:
With both Wikipedia and Creative Commons turning 25 this year, our participation in Wikimania 2026 felt especially meaningful. A quarter-century in, both organizations have evolved from scrappy experiments to global infrastructure. Our community has grown through a shared commitment to openness, access, and knowledge. The weeklong conference reaffirmed that commitment as AI is reshaping how we access knowledge and share online.

During the conference, CC hosted both a pre-conference salon celebrating our 25th Anniversary and a workshop during the main conference discussing collective action in the age of AI. CC staff also spoke on multiple panels throughout the week that addressed the effects of AI crawling on human creativity and sharing, the coordination gap between cultural institutions and generative AI, and training on CC’s global advocacy for the Open Heritage Statement.
